content_voiceover: Bernard Soulier syndrome results from a lack of the glycoprotein GPIb IX complex, more precisely a deficiency of the GPIb IX V complex, which you can see illustrated in the diagram sitting on the platelet membrane. This complex is the platelet's primary receptor for von Willebrand factor, and it also interacts with collagen, factor eleven, factor twelve, thrombin, thrombospondin, and kininogen, so when it is missing, platelets cannot properly adhere to the vessel wall under high shear conditions. Clinically this translates into two hallmark laboratory findings, a decreased platelet count, so this is a true thrombocytopenia unlike Glanzmann thrombasthenia, and large platelets greater than four micrometers in diameter on the peripheral smear. On aggregation studies, remember that Bernard Soulier syndrome shows absent aggregation specifically in response to ristocetin, while aggregation to other agonists like ADP and collagen remains normal, this is the opposite pattern from Glanzmann thrombasthenia and is a classic board discriminator.
keypoints: Bernard Soulier syndrome is caused by GPIb IX V complex deficiency
GPIb IX V is the platelet receptor for von Willebrand factor
Presents with decreased platelet count, unlike Glanzmann thrombasthenia
Large platelets greater than 4 micrometers on peripheral smear
Absent ristocetin induced aggregation but normal response to other agonists
keypoint_voiceover: Remember Bernard Soulier syndrome as GPIb IX V deficiency causing loss of von Willebrand factor binding. It presents with a low platelet count and giant platelets, and on aggregation studies it fails only with ristocetin, the mirror image of Glanzmann thrombasthenia.
